wrong: A photon with twice the bandgap energy frees two electrons.
right: One absorbed photon creates **one** electron–hole pair. The energy above $E_G$ is lost as heat (thermalisation).
tip: For every photon and every cell, ask one question: is $E_{\mathrm{ph}} \geq E_G$?

wrong: Brighter light means more energetic photons.
right: Photon energy depends only on wavelength ($hc/\lambda$). Brighter light means **more** photons per second, not stronger ones.

wrong: Two lamps with the same irradiance deliver the same number of photons.
right: At equal W/m², the longer-wavelength lamp delivers more photons, because each photon carries less energy: $\Phi = I\lambda/(hc)$.

wrong: In exercise 5.6(b) I can keep λ in nm and $hc$ in J m.
right: Make the length units match in **every** term: either λ² in m² and $P$ in W m⁻³, or $hc = 1.986 \times 10^{-16}$ J nm. Mixing them is off by 10⁹.
tip: In part (a) the nm cancel by themselves; in part (b) they don’t.

wrong: Photon flux and photon flux density are the same unit.
right: Strictly, flux is photons per second (s⁻¹) and flux density also per m² (m⁻² s⁻¹). The course uses ‘photon flux’ loosely: check whether the unit has m⁻².

wrong: In Snell’s law the angle in air always goes with n₁.
right: The subscripts only label the two sides. Pair each $n$ with the angle **in that same material**, measured from the normal.

wrong: Through a coating the ray angle stays the same in every layer.
right: The **product** $n\sin\theta$ stays the same; the angles differ (e.g. 16.3° in Si, 46.4° in MgF₂, 90° in air). Substitute the product, never the angle.

wrong: Light hitting silicon from air at more than 16.3° cannot enter.
right: Light can always enter from air. The critical angle is about **leaving** the denser medium: only rays inside the escape cone get out.

wrong: A coating changes the angle needed for total internal reflection at the front.
right: Because $n\sin\theta$ is conserved through parallel layers, the coating drops out: only the absorber and the final medium (air) set the threshold, 16.3° for c-Si.
tip: Write the chain $n_{\mathrm{Si}}\sin\theta_{\mathrm{BR}} = n_c\sin\theta_c = n_{\mathrm{air}}\sin 90°$ and let the middle term cancel.

wrong: I always use the full Fresnel equations, also at 0°.
right: At 0° (normal incidence) they reduce to $R = ((n_1 - n_2)/(n_1 + n_2))^2$. Read the angle in the question first; and keep full precision: rounding 0.562 to 0.56 turns 31.6 % into 31.4 %.

wrong: The reflectance is $r_s$ (or the average of $r_s$ and $r_p$).
right: $r_s$ and $r_p$ are **amplitude** ratios. Power goes with the square: $R = \frac{1}{2}(r_s^2 + r_p^2)$.

wrong: In the tandem, the bottom cell’s light is reduced by R₁, R₂ and R₃.
right: List the interfaces each photon actually crosses before multiplying (1 − R) factors. In instruction 1 Q2, LED Y crosses R₁, R₃ and R₄; R₂ belongs to experiment 2 only.

wrong: The path through the wafer is $d/\cos\theta_i$.
right: Inside the silicon the ray travels at $\theta_t$, so the path is $d/\cos\theta_t$, and it is one way (double it for the round trip).

wrong: Doubling the thickness doubles the absorption.
right: Lambert–Beer is exponential: each layer absorbs the same **fraction** of what is left. 50 % per pass becomes 75 % for two passes.

wrong: The Sun at 60° elevation gives AM2.
right: AM = 1/cos θ with θ measured from the **zenith**. 60° from the zenith (30° above the horizon) is AM2; 60° elevation is AM 1.15.

wrong: A solar cell consumes the energy of sunlight.
right: Energy is conserved. The cell diverts part of the energy flowing from the hot Sun to cold space into electrical energy; the rest becomes heat or is reflected.
